analysis.one_liner: Restores federal oversight of election changes in places with recent voting discrimination records and requires public notice of voting rule changes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2014 with 12 Democratic cosponsors, the Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings in June and December 2014 but the bill never reached a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court struck down the old coverage formula in the Voting Rights Act in June 2013, this bill would have written a new one: any state with 5 or more recent voting-rights violations, or any county or town with 3 or more, would have had to get federal approval before changing its voting rules. It also required state and local election offices to publicly announce changes to voting procedures, polling place staffing, and district boundaries within 48 hours, and made it easier for voters to get a court order blocking a discriminatory change. The bill never made it out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially Black, Hispanic, Asian American, and Native American voters — in states and localities with recent records of voting discrimination, who would regain federal review of election changes and get public notice when polling places, machines, or district lines change. Language-minority voters would gain access to federal observers enforcing bilingual election requirements.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new coverage formula tied to actual conduct: a state is covered if it had 5 or more voting-rights violations in the previous 15 years, at least one by the state itself; a county or municipality is covered with 3 or more violations, or 1 violation plus persistently very low minority turnout [S2][S3].

Requires election offices to give public notice within 48 hours of changes to voting procedures, and to post data on polling place locations, machines, and poll workers before federal elections, so last-minute changes are visible rather than discovered on Election Day [S3].

Lets any aggrieved voter — not just the Attorney General — ask a court to block a discriminatory voting change, and directs courts to weigh the hardship to voters when deciding whether to block a change adopted shortly before an election [S3].
Expands federal observer authority, including observers assigned specifically to enforce bilingual election requirements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local election offices in covered jurisdictions bear the cost and burden of pre-clearing voting changes with federal authorities, and all larger jurisdictions bear new public-notice and data-reporting duties. Jurisdictions with violation records lose the freedom to change voting rules without federal review.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves photo ID laws out of the process: violations based on requiring photo identification do not count toward covering a jurisdiction, and courts' jurisdiction-retention authority does not extend to photo ID cases, a major concession to supporters of such laws [S3].

The transparency section only requires notice — it does not stop a jurisdiction from making a change, so voters learn about polling closures or rule changes but cannot prevent them through this section alone [S3].

Election offices in covered jurisdictions would face real administrative costs: preparing data filings on precincts, machines, and poll workers, and publicizing every change within 48 hours, a burden small local offices would feel most [S3].

A conduct-based coverage formula depends on litigation and Justice Department enforcement to generate the 'violations' that trigger coverage, so under-enforcement in a region could keep it off the covered list.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters in jurisdictions with records of discrimination, the bill would have restored a meaningful check — federal review before election changes take effect — at a modest administrative cost to local election offices. Its honest weaknesses are the photo ID carve-out, which exempts the most debated modern voting restriction from coverage, and the fact that transparency alone notifies rather than prevents. It was a deliberately middle-ground response to the Court's decision, and even so it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee: hearings were held in June and December 2014, but the committee never voted to send it to the floor, and the Congress ended in January 2015 with no Senate vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the Voting Rights Amendment Act of 2014 on January 16, 2014, joined by Senators Durbin and Coons [S1][S3].
Twelve Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
The full Judiciary Committee held a hearing on June 25, 2014, and its Constitution subcommittee held another on December 9, 2014, but the committee never reported the bill [S5].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with no floor vote in either chamber; the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local officials who wanted no new federal review of election changes are better off; jurisdictions that would have been covered under the new formula avoid pre-clearance, and no election office faces the new notice and reporting duties.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and chaired the Judiciary Committee hearing held on it in June 2014

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings in June and December 2014 but never voted the bill out of committee, leaving it no path to the floor

against.name: 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support its sponsors sought and no committee majority to advance it

sides.party_line_note: All 13 Senate supporters — the sponsor and 12 cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: Covered jurisdictions would have had to get federal approval before changing voting rules, and larger jurisdictions would face 48-hour public notice and detailed data-reporting duties on precincts, machines, and poll workers. Their interest in avoiding federal oversight runs against voters' interest in having last-minute changes reviewed and disclosed.

industries.industry: Jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violation records
industries.note: States with 5 or more violations in 15 years, and subdivisions with 3 or more, would have been subject to pre-clearance of voting changes. The bill would have shifted the cost of proving fairness onto the jurisdictions with the worst recent records.
